- When sentiment is consistently bearish (negative or low) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, adjust downward by 2–5% to account for suppressed demand or policy-induced sell-off.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days to avoid overshoot.  
- If official event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model underestimates downside risk — add 3–8% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish mid-period, model often fails to pivot — apply a “sentiment lag” correction: reduce forecast by 1–3% per day for 3–5 days post-shift.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 consecutive days below 50% of 30d mean), model overestimates trend — apply a “mean reversion” rule: cap forecast at 1.5x prior 14d average.  
- If official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model tends to overestimate price stability — reduce forecast by 1–3% per event day to reflect supply pressure.
